scienceObservations.criterion: Constant angular speed and initial phase
scienceObservations.observation: Uniform rotation at omega_0 and positive-axis alignment at t=0 imply phi(0)=0 and x(0)=x_m. The cosine is not generalized to an arbitrary starting direction without a phase offset.
Phi=omega_0 t counts elapsed rotation continuously. The smaller angle between lines is explicitly excluded; no periodic resetting of phi is implied.

Radius magnitude equals amplitude, accumulated angle is expressed in time, then x=x_m cos(phi)=x_m cos(omega_0 t) yields harmonic projection. Negative cosine represents displacement on the other side of equilibrium, not a negative physical radius.
The harmonic statement concerns the signed coordinate or shadow. The ball continues around its circular path rather than oscillating along the screen axis.

Parallel rays in the disk plane and a screen normal to those rays preserve the relevant vertical component in the illustrated setup. The text does not substitute divergent illumination or claim an arbitrary screen orientation gives the same displacement.

O_1X is retained, not replaced with a horizontal axis merely because its coordinate is called x. The shadow displacement is vertical and measured from the projected center O_1; the spring comparison uses each system's equilibrium position.

scienceObservations.criterion: Equal amplitude, equilibrium height, frequency and phase
scienceObservations.observation: The setup aligns equilibrium shadow heights, sets spring release displacement equal to the ball-path radius, matches rotation frequency to oscillation frequency, and starts both at their upper extrema. Release without a push is consistent with starting at an extremum. No numerical equality between angular speed in radians per second and frequency in cycles per second is asserted.

The stated linear restoring force and negligible resistance supply the ideal harmonic approximation over the observation. Negligible resistance expresses the required negligible damping; the conclusion is preceded by these conditions, not applied universally to nonlinear or appreciably damped springs.

Choosing the disk rate matches a separately oscillating spring. The explicit no-drive sentence rules out a coupling inference, and illustrates accurately carries the approved Chinese demonstration rather than claiming the disk generates the spring motion.

The text uses symbolic radius/amplitude and experimental preparation only. It does not extract a numerical angle, radius, period, frequency or height from a schematic, nor claim static extrema establish time-dependent synchronization.

readabilityObservations.childReaderJudgment: For a child reading this unit with its preceding oscillation and cosine vocabulary, the prose is clear enough to follow the derivation and the experiment. This is an editorial reading judgment, not a measured age score or user study.
readabilityObservations.concreteLanguage: Back-and-forth, upward and downward, shadow, same height, without an extra push and uppermost positions connect the abstract quantities to observable actions.
readabilityObservations.sentenceAndParagraphLoad: Short sentences and focused paragraphs separate setup, formula, interpretation and conditions. The long original spring object becomes five manageable paragraphs rather than a single dense explanation.
readabilityObservations.technicalVocabulary: Projection is introduced as the corresponding position on an axis, its sign is tied to side of equilibrium, and phase is tied to starting alignment. The necessary mathematical vocabulary is retained rather than replaced with a misleading simplification.
readabilityObservations.remainingPrerequisites: Cosine, vector notation, equilibrium and the spring restoring-force concept are still course prerequisites. The lesson does not purport to be a standalone introduction to all of them.
readabilityObservations.conclusionClarity: The bold sentence names the spring weight and the ball's shadow explicitly. The following no-drive explanation prevents same displacement law from being read as a mechanical drive relationship.
